newsitem.title: UK: UK says N. Ireland Sinn Fein talks ban remains.
newsitem.headline: UK says N. Ireland Sinn Fein talks ban remains.

text.p: The British government said on Tuesday there had been no change to its ban on official talks with the IRA's political wing, Sinn Fein, despite renewed contacts between officials and the Irish republican group.
Leading Loyalist politicians, who want to keep the province British, said they did not think the contacts with Sinn Fein group would derail a Northern Ireland peace process.
"These contacts with Sinn Fein are to be expected, unfortunately," said David Ervine, leader of the Progressive Unionist Party, after talks with Prime Minister Tony Blair.
Britain and Ireland, co-sponsors of the talks, said a month ago they were severing official contacts with Sinn Fein because of the deaths of two policemen in an IRA daylight ambush.

But Northern Ireland Secretary Mo Mowlam, angering pro-British Unionists, acknowledged on Monday that officials had contacted Sinn Fein after the group sought clarification of the requirements for its admission to peace talks.
Mowlam came under pressure in parliament on Tuesday over her admission. Ulster Unionist security spokesman Ken Maginnis said Mowlam should explain whether there had been a change of policy.
But a spokeswoman for the Northern Ireland Office said: "There has been no change in policy because we have said there would be no meetings and there have not been any meetings."

She said the Northern Ireland Office had responded to demands from Sinn Fein for clarification of the requirements the republican group had to meet before being allowed into peace talks and on the question of the surrender of guerrilla arms.
"At no point could this be seen as a negotiation," she said.
Blair has said Sinn Fein can only join peace talks if it persuades its Irish Republican Army allies to call a new truce.

But in an attempt to give new impetus to the talks which bogged down in the dying days of John Major's ousted Conservative government, Blair has said the group could join the talks as soon as six weeks after a ceasefire.
The peace talks resumed on Tuesday with preliminary discussions before a plenary session on Wednesday.
The row over the government's contacts with Sinn Fein has cast a cloud over the talks.

But after talks with Blair in London on Tuesday, the politicians with links to loyalist paramilitary groups -- so-called because they are "loyal" to British rule -- said the row would not derail the process. "I'm not particularly dismayed, I don't think it matters a damn," said Ervine.
Tension remains high in Northern Ireland after the end of the most sensitive week in the province's political calendar.
A Protestant Orange Order parade down the Catholic Garvaghy Road area of Portadown nine days ago sparked nights of violence and prompted Catholics to threaten mass counter demonstrations.
Five days ago the pro-British Orange Order eased Catholic anger by deciding not to route four of its marches through Catholic areas on its most cherished anniversary.
But hopes this would bring an equivalent gesture from nationalists were dashed when an Orange Order hall near Pomeroy, 50 miles (80 km) west of Belfast was burnt out early on Tuesday.

Police were also investigating the death of a Catholic girl on Tuesday. The 18-year-old girl was sleeping at a house in the staunchly Protestant village of Aghalee some 30 miles (50 km) southwest of Belfast when a gunman shot her in the head.

A man was arrested locally. Police said they did not know whether the killing was sectarian. Ervine said he was unaware of the shooting, telling reporters: "I know nothing of it. But it's another life gone, one more too many."
